prompt: A bug bounty report came in for this document-sharing service: a researcher read another user's files and wrote files outside their own folder. That is all the detail we have. Please close the holes without breaking normal use. The four exported handlers in src/handlers.js are uploadFile(storageRoot, userId, input), downloadFile(storageRoot, userId, input), listFolder(storageRoot, userId, input) and importArchive(storageRoot, userId, input); each returns a promise for { status, body }, and keeps doing so. Every caller must stay inside their own account folder, whatever path, file name or archive entry they send. Upload names are single file names, and an upload must not replace an existing file unless the caller passes overwrite: true. Error responses must not reveal storage paths or other accounts. Normal use must keep working: nested folders, unicode names, names with several dots such as report..final.pdf, and archives with nested folders in the format src/archive.js reads. Keep the response shapes, the archive format, the CommonJS API and the no-dependency setup.

rubric.criterion: The fix contains every path at one shared place (resolve, then check the result stays under the caller's folder) instead of filtering bad strings, and the final message says which routes were open (download, list, upload name, archive entry) and how each is now closed. Fail: blocks only "../" strings or patches handlers one by one, or does not say what was open. Partial: one shared containment check, but the message misses a route (for example absolute archive entries or symlinks) or the check is skipped on one handler. Pass: one shared containment check used by all four handlers, each open route named with how it is closed, and errors that reveal no storage path. (code cannot check this because the hidden probes show the holes are shut, not whether the fix is one coherent rule a reviewer can trust)

items.text: Puts the containment check in one shared function used by every handler (resolve, then compare with a separator-aware prefix or a relative-path test), so a new handler cannot skip it.
Explains that the check must run after all decoding and normalisation, and why checking the raw string first is not enough.

Notes the gap between checking a path and opening it (a symlink can be swapped in between) and how the fix handles it, for example by refusing links when opening or checking the real path of the opened file.
Mentions archive limits beyond names: entry count, total unpacked size and link entries, against archive bombs and link tricks.
Suggests storing uploads under generated names with the user's name kept as metadata, as a stronger long-term design than validating names.
Logs the rejected path on the server for investigation while the response stays generic.

verdicts.note: The prompt describes the deliverable (security fixes) and the constraints without prescribing a named method, framework, or process for how to work.

All behaviors tested are explicitly stated in the prompt: reject separators in upload names, prevent traversal via decoded paths and absolute paths, avoid following symlinks, prevent overwrites without the flag, and keep error messages generic.
The fixture contains no comments, documentation, or tests that reveal the vulnerabilities or their fixes; it only shows normal usage patterns.

Reviewer flagged checks that required O_NOFOLLOW and path.relative in the source; the lead removed them. The draft prompt also listed each attack (encoded dots, backslashes, symlinks, archive names); the lead cut it to the bounty report plus the rules. 4 of 20 hidden tests pass on the fixture.

All hidden tests are fair requirements explicitly stated in the prompt: block traversal attacks, handle encoded paths, reject separators in upload names, prevent overwrites, avoid symlink escapes, and hide internal paths in errors.

items.note: The prompt describes the bug class (path traversal) as reported, the required behavior, and the constraints, without naming a method, tool, or checklist to use.
Fixture files show vulnerable code patterns but never state the specific attack vectors or fixes; evidence must be reasoned from the handlers.
Hidden tests check path traversal variants (../, encoded, absolute paths, symlinks) that directly exploit the vulnerable resolve() calls in fixture/src/handlers.js.
The prompt explains the vulnerability class and required constraints; a careful engineer can analyze handlers.js to see the unsafe path.resolve() calls and fix them.
